implementation_notes: Spring Statemachine provides the decider as a configured state chart (states, transitions, guards, actions) and persistence through StateMachinePersist plus the data-jpa/data-redis modules, so an instance is restored from the store, fed the reply, and written back after the transition. Guards and actions keep the flow declarative instead of a switch, and the reference documents timers as triggers that a scheduler sends for deadlines. Choose it when the flow is a genuine state chart inside one service and Spring is already the platform; when the steps are remote services owned by other teams, the same shape is usually better expressed with a durable workflow engine.
pitfalls: A state machine is not a shared singleton: obtain one machine per process instance from the factory and restore it with the persister before sending an event.
The persister runs per transition and is not transactional with your own database writes unless it is wired into the same transaction; a crash in between repeats a step.
Guards and actions that block (remote calls, I/O) hold the machine's thread and defeat the concurrency the framework assumes.

variants.name: Temporal workflow (durable execution)
variants.implementation_notes: The workflow method is the process manager and the server owns the state: every await is recorded in history, so the flow survives worker restarts, can sleep for days, and resumes exactly where it stopped. Activities hold the side effects and their retry policies, deadlines use Workflow.await(timeout, condition) or timers, and compensation is ordinary code on the failure path (the SDK ships saga examples). Choose it over an in-process state chart when the flow spans services and must outlive deployments; determinism rules - no direct I/O, clock and randomness only through the SDK - are the price of that durability.
pitfalls: Non-deterministic workflow code (System.currentTimeMillis, raw threads, direct HTTP) fails replay; the SDK's clock and sleep functions exist for that reason.
Activities are retried by default, so a non-idempotent payment activity can charge twice unless it carries a business key or an explicit retry policy.
Cancelling a workflow does not undo completed activities; compensation must be coded or a cancellation handler must run it.
